definition: Treating all sides fairly, without favoring one person or group over another.
example: The science fair needed impartial judges who had never met any of the students.
nuance: Impartial means free of bias, not uninterested: an impartial judge can care a great deal about reaching a fair result.
prompt: A referee is officiating a championship game between two rival schools.
options: The impartial referee judged both teams' fouls by the same standard.
The impartial referee overlooked every foul committed by her hometown team.
The impartial referee got so bored that she stopped watching the second half.
Because she read every single rule aloud, her review of the rulebook was impartial.
reasons: Applying one rule equally to both sides is exactly what fairness without favoritism looks like.
Letting one side off the hook is favoritism, the reverse of the word's meaning.
This confuses fairness with lack of interest; not paying attention is indifference.
The word is about fairness, not completeness; reading every rule shows thoroughness.

practice.prompt: A teacher must grade a stack of essays, and one of them was written by her nephew.
options: She was so impartial about grading that the stack sat untouched for a week.
She finished only an impartial batch, so half the essays still had no grades.
To stay impartial, she covered the names on each essay before grading it.
Being impartial, she quietly added two bonus points to her nephew's score.
reasons: Neglecting the work reflects not caring, which is different from being fair.
This mistakes the word for partial, meaning incomplete; it has nothing to do with amount.
Hiding who wrote each essay keeps family ties from influencing the grades.
Giving a relative extra credit shows favoritism, which the word rules out.
